senses.gloss:
Mīmāṁsā Darśana
------------------------------------------
Introduction
If there is any system of Hindu philosophy where the Book becomes more important than the Maker of the Book, it is the Mīmāṁsā. Also called Pūrva-मीमाṁसा दर्शन, it primarily aims at giving a methodology of interpretation with the help of which complicated Vedic injunctions regarding rituals may be understood and given effect to.
Vedic ritualism believes that:
there is a सोउल् which survives the death of the body and enjoys the fruits of the rituals in हेअवेन्;
there is a शक्ति or power of potency which preserves the effects of the rituals performed;
the वेदस् are infallible;
this world is real;
our life and actions performed here are real and not mere द्रेअम्स्.
Basic Works
The Mīmāṁsāsūtras of जैमिनि (200 B. C.) is the basic text of this system. It is a voluminous work comprising more than 2500 aphorisms divided into 12 chapters and 60 subsections in all.
The Bhāṣya of Śabara Svāmin (57 B. C. or A. D. 200) gives the most authoritative interpretation of the sūtras. Śabara’s Bhāṣya has two commentaries. The Bṛhatī of प्रभाकर (A. D. 650), still in the manuscript form, is the first. The second is by कुमारिल भट्ट (A. D. 700) in three parts: Ślokavārttika, Tantra-vārttika and Ṭupṭīkā. Prakaraṇapañcikā of Śālikanātha (a pupil of प्रभाकर), Śāstradīpikā of Pārthasarathi (A. D. 900), Nyāyamālāvistara of Mādhava विद्यारण्य (A. D. 1350) and Arthasaṅgraha of Laugākṣi भास्कर (17th cent. A. D.) are some of the other works of this system.
Theory of Knowledge
To justify the supreme authority of the वेदस्, the मीमाṁसा दर्शन has developed an elaborate epistemology which has been accepted by other schools also, especially the वेदान्त दर्शन.
For knowledge to be valid, three conditions have to be fulfilled. They are:
It should yield some new information previously unknown.
It should not be contradicted by any other knowledge.
The conditions which generate that knowledge should be free from defects.
The Mīmāṁsā admits of two kinds of knowledge: प्रत्यक्ष (immediate) and परोक्ष (mediate).
The latter, again, is of five kinds: अनुमान (inference), उपमान (comparison), शब्द (verbal testimony, also called ‘āptavākya’, words of a reliable person), अर्थापत्ति (postulation) and अनुपलब्धि (non-perception).
These may now be briefly described.
PRATYAKṢA (direct or immediate perception) has two stages of development. As soon as the sense-organ comes into contact with the sense-object, there is a general awareness of it, as something existing. This is called निर्विकल्पक-प्रत्यक्ष. In the next stage, all the details will be noted in the light of past experience. This is सविकल्पक-प्रत्यक्ष.
ANUMĀNA (inference) gives us the knowledge of a thing indirectly, when we see some लिङ्ग or sign invariably connected with the original. For instance, by seeing smoke on a yonder hill, we can infer that there is fire there (even though we do not see it directly), since it is known from previous observations and experience that smoke is invariably associated with fire.
UPAMĀNA (comparison) is another source of knowledge. On seeing a rat, one recollects that it is like the mouse he had seen earlier. He then comes to know that the remembered mouse is like the perceived rat. This type of knowledge comes through उपमान.
ŚABDA (verbal testimony) is the next source of knowledge. The मीमाṁसा दर्शन pays the greatest attention to this since it has to justify the undisputed authority of the वेदस्.
The words of a reliable person are believed to be true. This is called āptavākya.
Verbal testimony, however, is of two types: pauruṣeya (personal, same as āptavākya) and apauruṣeya (impersonal). The second denotes the वेदस् since they were not created by any human agency. The वेदस् are supremely authoritative since they are the ‘Book of Commandments’ and also give us authentic know-ledge of the unseen and the unknown truths. Again, their main purport and purpose lies in propagating sacrificial rites.
The वेदस् are eternal, not as the printed Book nor as the orally transmitted mantras but as the eternal teachings contained in them. These teachings are conveyed through the ṛṣis or sages in every age.
Since the वेदस् are mainly concerned with giving commands (= विधि) about the yāgas or sacrificial rites and other associated rituals, only those sentences containing such commands as expressed through the verbs couched in ‘vidhiliṅ’ (imperative mood as in ‘svargakāmo yajeta’, ‘One desirous of attaining हेअवेन् should sacrifice!’) and other forms should be taken as authoritative and others as aids to it. Such verbs have an innate power of urging the hearer to do the sacrifice. This is called ‘bhāvanā’. The urge contained in the Vedic words is known as ‘śābdībhāvanā’ (śabda = word). On hearing it, the person who hears it, gets the urge to perform it. This secondary urge is named ‘ārthībhāvanā’ (artha = utility, useful activity).
All this depends upon the correct understanding and interpretation of the Vedic sentences. For this, the Mīmāṁsā gives six steps: उपक्रम (beginning) and upasaṁhāra (concluding); अभ्यास (repetition for the sake of emphasis); apūrvatā (not being known earlier by any other means); phala (utility); अर्थवाद (mere eulogy) and upapatti (logic and reasoning).
Once the correct meaning is thus ascertained, the command can be implemented.
ARTHĀPATTI (postulation or presumption) is the necessary supposition of an unperceived fact which alone can explain an anomaly satisfactorily. For instance, if a person is noticed to be getting fat even though he does not eat during the day, it can safely be presumed that he is secretly eating at night! Knowledge obtained by अर्थापत्ति is distinctive since it cannot be got by any other means.
ANUPALABDHI (non-perception) has also been accepted as a source of know-ledge since it gives the immediate चोग्नितिओन् of the non-existence of an object. If it is found that a jar which had been kept on a table earlier, is not perceived now, its non-existence is cognized.
Since the validity of knowledge that we get is an important aspect of our life, giving rise to necessary activities, this has been discussed in detail by the writers of Mīmāṁsā works.
Incidentally, they also discuss how errors creep in, giving their own explanations and theories. This has led to two different views.
When a snake is perceived in a rope in dim light, though the rope seen now and the snake seen in the past are both real, a mixing up takes place due to a lapse of memory giving rise to a reaction of fear. This is called akhyātivāda (denial of illusory perception).
In the second view known as viparīta-khyātivāda, the error consists in wrongly relating two really existing, but separate, entities.
Metaphysics
a) The World
Unlike some other systems (like Advaita Vedānta) the Mīmāṁsā believes in the reality of the world, with all the myriad objects in it. This world, according to it, comprises the living bodies including the various इन्द्रियस् or the sense-organs, wherein the souls reside temporarily to reap the effects of their karmas, good or bad. The various objects of the world serve as the fruits to be suffered or enjoyed.
b) The Soul
There are infinite number of souls. They are eternal but undergo transmigration due to their karmas (good or bad deeds) performed when encased in real bodies in a real world.
The सोउल् has no चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of its own. चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् rises in it due to association with the मिन्द्, the sense-organs and the sense-objects, especially when the organs come into contact with their respective objects. This is proved by the absence of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् in the deep-sleep state.
When a person performs Vedic sacri-fices like ज्योतिष्टोम, say to get to हेअवेन्, the potential effect of it in a subtle form resides in his सोउल् and will give its fruit after death. This potential imperceptible power or शक्ति, is called ‘apūrva’.
Since the whole of the वेदस् are meant to urge the human beings to perform karmas (Vedic rituals), every human being is bound to do his duty for duty’s sake. A ritual is to be done, only because the वेदस् command it and none has the choice not to do it or do it in a different way!
Such duties are classified into two broad groups: नित्य or daily obligatory duties and naimittika or occasional (but obligatory) duties. These help in the purification of the सोउल् through moral improvement.
c) मोक्ष or liberation
The highest good (niśśreyasa) for a person is to get मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्, total cessation of transmigratory existence. In this state the सोउल् is permanently free from all pain and suffering though there is no चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् or bliss!
The ultimate goal of life was, probably, according to the earlier conception of the Mīmāṁsā, the attainment of unalloyed bliss in हेअवेन्. However, the available literature does not support it.
How to attain मोक्ष?—is a question that has been answered in a rather simplistic way. Not performing kāmya-karmas or desire-motivated actions will not cause rebirth. Sins committed unwillingly can be offset by the performance of the various prāyaścittas (expiatory rites). Performance of नित्य and naimittika karmas will bring about cittaśuddhi or purity of मिन्द् whereas their non-performance will result in pratyavāyadoṣa or the error of omission, proving to be an obstacle in the path of मोक्ष. प्रारब्धकर्म (karma that has caused this birth) is exhausted by experience in this life. So, when the body falls, there is no residual factor that can bring the सोउल् back to this world once again. Consequently लिबेरतिओन् is attained automatically.
d) ईश्वर or God
Another question that is discussed and discarded by the Mīmāṁsā system is whether ईश्वर or God exists or not. Since all the materials that make up the physical world are eternally existing and since the adṛṣṭas or the karmas of the souls impel these materials in the process of च्रेअतिओन्, there is no need to accept any God as the agent or author of च्रेअतिओन्.
Epilogue
It is rather strange that a system that champions the supremacy of the वेदस् goes to the extent of enthroning the Book as God, and, dethrone and abandon its maker! Let alone God, even the various deities like इन्द्र, मित्र and वरुण who are invoked in the sacrificial rites to receive the offerings, are treated more like the imaginary characters of a fictitious drama.
It may not be wrong to declare that by overemphasizing the means to the detriment of the end, the Mīmāṁsā dug its own grave as a living system of philosophy.
However, an earnest study of its theory of knowledge as also its method of interpreting the Vedic sentences will be of great help in understanding the Vedāntic systems better.
